field.name: description
field.div: Set up Odoo for development, create your first module and build its screens: list, form, search, calendar and activity views, then menus and actions that open them. By the end you have the base of the om_hospital app running in your own database.

div.p: Before you write any code, you need an Odoo that runs from its source, in an editor where you can read and debug it. This section sets that up once, and you reuse it for every lesson.

ul.li: Get the Odoo source, create a Python virtual environment and install the packages of requirements.txt.
Install PostgreSQL and create a database user for Odoo.
Open the project in PyCharm and run odoo-bin from a run configuration.
Add a folder of your own modules to the addons path, next to the standard odoo/addons and addons folders. This is where om_hospital lives.
Start Odoo from the terminal with options, and save these options in a configuration file.
Let Odoo restart by itself when a Python file changes, and stop on a breakpoint with the debugger.

div.p: Odoo reads its options from a file given with -c. A small file for local development:

pre.code: [options] admin_passwd = admin db_host = localhost db_port = 5432 db_user = odoo db_password = odoo http_port = 8069 addons_path = /path/to/odoo/odoo/addons,/path/to/odoo/addons,/path/to/custom_addons

div.p: Then start Odoo with it, and turn on the developer options you need:

pre.code: python3 odoo-bin -c odoo.conf -d hospital_db --dev=reload,xml

div.p: --dev=reload restarts the server when a Python file is saved. --dev=xml reads views from the XML files, so most view changes show after a page refresh. A change in a model (a new field) or in a data file still needs a module upgrade.
Once Odoo runs and you can log in to a database, you are ready to create your first module.

record.field: Where does Odoo look for the modules it can install?
In the folders listed in the addons path
Odoo scans each folder of addons_path for modules with a __manifest__.py.
In every folder of the Python virtual environment
The virtual environment holds Python packages, not Odoo modules.
Only in the odoo/addons folder of the source
That folder is one entry of the addons path; you add your own folders next to it.
You changed a Python method and Odoo runs with --dev=reload. What happens?
The server restarts by itself and the new code runs
reload watches the Python files and restarts the server when one is saved.
Nothing until you upgrade the module
An upgrade is needed for new fields and data files, not to reload Python code with --dev=reload.
Restarting the server never touches the data in the database.
What is the configuration file for?
To keep the server options (database user, ports, addons path...) in one place
You start Odoo with -c and the file, instead of typing every option each time.
To store the records of the database
Records are stored in PostgreSQL, not in the configuration file.
To list the modules to install in each database
Modules are installed per database, from the Apps menu or with -i.
To declare the models of a module
Models are Python classes in the modules themselves.
Why run Odoo in the PyCharm debugger while you learn?
To stop on a line of your code and look at the records and variables at that moment
A breakpoint shows you what the code really receives, which is faster than guessing.
Because Odoo does not start without a debugger
Odoo starts fine from the terminal; the debugger is a help, not a requirement.
The debugger makes Odoo slower; use it only when you need it.

div.p: An Odoo module is a folder in your addons path with a manifest. In this section you create om_hospital, install it and upgrade it each time you change it.

ul.li: __manifest__.py: the name, version, dependencies (mail, sale) and the list of data files to load, in order.
__init__.py and models/__init__.py: import the Python files.
models/patient.py: the model hospital.patient with fields such as name, date_of_birth, gender and tag_ids.
security/ir.model.access.csv: who may read, write, create and delete each model.
views/patient_views.xml and views/menus.xml: the screens and the menus.
static/description/icon.png: the icon shown in Apps and on the home screen.

pre.code:
from odoo import fields, models
class HospitalPatient(models.Model): _name = 'hospital.patient' _inherit = ['mail.thread', 'mail.activity.mixin'] _description = 'Hospital Patient'
name = fields.Char(required=True, tracking=True) date_of_birth = fields.Date() gender = fields.Selection([('male', 'Male'), ('female', 'Female'), ('other', 'Other')], required=True, default='male', tracking=True)

div.p: Each new model needs a line in the access file, or only the superuser can use it:

pre.code: id,name,model_id:id,group_id:id,perm_read,perm_write,perm_create,perm_unlink access_hospital_patient_user,hospital.patient user,model_hospital_patient,base.group_user,1,1,1,1

div.p: Install the module once with -i, then upgrade it with -u after you add a field, a view or a data file:

pre.code: python3 odoo-bin -c odoo.conf -d hospital_db -i om_hospital python3 odoo-bin -c odoo.conf -d hospital_db -u om_hospital

div.p: Odoo creates the database table hospital_patient from the model, and loads the XML and CSV files listed in data of the manifest.

record.field: What makes a folder an Odoo module?
A __manifest__.py file, in a folder that is in the addons path
The manifest describes the module; the addons path lets Odoo find it.
A models folder with at least one model
A module can have no model at all, for example a module with only views or data.
A line for it in the configuration file
The configuration file lists addons folders, not single modules.
You added a model but users see an access error. What is missing?
A line for the model in security/ir.model.access.csv, loaded by the manifest
Without an access rule, only the superuser can use the model.
The model is not in the menu
A missing menu hides the model; it does not raise an access error.
A restart without an upgrade does not create access rights.
You added a new field to hospital.patient and a new XML file. What must you do?
Add the XML file to data in the manifest, then upgrade the module with -u
The upgrade adds the column to the table and loads the files listed in the manifest.
A restart loads the Python code, but the column and the new view are created by an upgrade.
Uninstall and install the module again
That works but deletes the data of the module; an upgrade is enough.
Why does om_hospital list mail in depends?
Its models inherit mail.thread and mail.activity.mixin, which come from mail
A module must depend on every module whose models or views it uses.
To send e-mails when the module is installed
Depending on a module only makes its code available; it sends nothing.
Because every module must depend on mail
Most modules depend on base or other modules; mail is needed only for chatter and activities.

div.p: Views decide how records are shown. They are XML records of the model ir.ui.view, in views/patient_views.xml, views/appointment_views.xml and views/doctor_views.xml. One model can have several views; the action decides which ones the user can switch between.

ul.li: List and form for patients, doctors and appointments, with a notebook, a status bar, buttons and the chatter (messages, followers, activities).
Search view: fields to search on, filters, group by, and a search panel on gender.
Kanban for patients, calendar and activity views for appointments.
Widgets: badge and decorations on state, priority, many2many_tags, statinfo in a stat button.

pre.code: <header> <button name="action_confirm" string="Confirm" type="object" class="btn-primary" invisible="state != 'draft'"/> <field name="state" widget="statusbar" statusbar_visible="draft,confirm,done"/> </header> ... <field name="patient_id" readonly="state != 'draft'"/> <field name="date_appointment" required="state == 'confirm'"/>

<tree multi_edit="1" sample="1" decoration-muted="state == 'cancel'"> <field name="name"/> <field name="priority" widget="priority" optional="show"/> <field name="state" widget="badge" decoration-success="state == 'done'"/> </tree>

Since 17, invisible takes a Python expression on the fields of the record.

Remove the button in Python when the state changes

What does the search panel on gender in the patient search view do?
It shows a side panel with the gender values, and clicking one filters the records
A searchpanel lists the values of a field and filters by them, with counters if enabled.
It makes gender required in the form
Search views never change how a form behaves.
It groups the list by gender by default
That is a group by filter, set with search_default_ in the context.
A model has a list, a form and a calendar view. What decides which ones the user can switch between?
The view_mode of the action that opens the model
The action lists the view types, e.g. tree,form,calendar (list,form,calendar from 18).
The order of the records in the XML file
The order of views in files does not make them available.
_inherit adds features to the model; it does not list views.
Why does the appointment calendar need a model that has a date or datetime field?
date_start tells the calendar where to place each record
Without a start date the calendar cannot draw the event.
Because calendar views only work for the calendar module
Any model with a date field can have a calendar view.
A calendar view only displays records; it does not send anything.
Actions and menus: how screens open

div.p: A menu does nothing by itself: it opens an action. The action says what to show: a model in some views (a window action), a web page (a URL action), some Python code (a server action) or a client action such as a notification.
div.h4: Menus and window actions in om_hospital
div.p: The menus are in views/menus.xml, the actions next to their views. action_hospital_female shows a domain and a context together:

pre.code:
<record id="action_hospital_female" model="ir.actions.act_window"> <field name="name">Female Patients</field> <field name="res_model">hospital.patient</field> <field name="view_mode">tree,kanban,form</field> <field name="domain">[('gender', '=', 'female')]</field> <field name="context">{'default_gender': 'female', 'hide_gender': True}</field> </record>
<menuitem id="menu_female" name="Female Patients" parent="menu_patient_root" action="action_hospital_female" sequence="30"/>

ul.li: The domain filters the records: only female patients are listed.
default_gender in the context fills the field on new records; hide_gender is read by the form with invisible="context.get('hide_gender')".
menu_sale_appointment puts an om_hospital action under an existing Sales menu.

record.field: What happens when a user clicks a menu that has an action?
Odoo runs the action, for example opens the model in the views of its view_mode
Menus only point to actions; the action decides what is shown.
Odoo opens the form of the model named like the menu

What is the difference between the domain and the context of action_hospital_female?
The domain filters which records are shown; the context sets defaults and flags for the views
default_gender fills new records; the domain limits the list to female patients.

A UserError shows an error dialog and rolls back the transaction.

What does binding_model_id do on a server action?
It adds the action to the Action menu of that model's views

It chooses the model the code may read
model_id sets the model of the action; the code can read any model through env.

Odoo Development: Fields and the ORM

field.name: description
field.div: Learn every common field type, from dates and relations to computed, monetary and image fields, and the business logic around them: create, write, unlink, constraints, copy and display names. Then use the ORM from Python and the shell, and build wizards with transient models.

div.p: Fields are the columns of your model. Each one is a Python attribute built from a class of odoo.fields, and Odoo creates the database column for it when you upgrade the module.

ul.li: models/patient.py (hospital.patient): name (Char), date_of_birth (Date), gender (Selection), image (Binary), responsible_id (Many2one to res.partner), tag_ids (Many2many to patient.tag), appointment_ids (One2many).
models/appointment.py (hospital.appointment): date_appointment (Datetime with a default), prescription (Html), fee (Monetary), age and gender (related to the patient).

div.p: A Many2one stores the id of one record of another model. A One2many is its reverse: it lists the records whose Many2one points to this record, so it needs the name of that Many2one. A Many2many links records on both sides through a relation table.

pre.code: responsible_id = fields.Many2one('res.partner', string='Responsible') tag_ids = fields.Many2many('patient.tag', string='Tags') appointment_ids = fields.One2many('hospital.appointment', 'patient_id', string='Appointments')

div.p: A computed field gets its value from a method. With store=True the value is saved in the database (so you can search and group on it) and recomputed when a field listed in @api.depends changes. A related field is a shortcut to a field of a linked record.

In appointment.py, age = fields.Integer(related='patient_id.age') shows the age of the patient, and fee = fields.Monetary(currency_field='currency_id') uses the related currency_id of the company. A compute method must always assign a value to every record, even when there is nothing to compute.

field.name: description
field.div: Protect your module with groups, access rights and record rules, extend existing Odoo models, views and methods with inheritance, and ship data and settings with your module.

div.p: Security in Odoo answers two questions: which models can a user read, write, create or delete, and which records of those models can he see. Odoo answers them with three building blocks:

ul.li: Groups (res.groups): a set of users, for example Hospital / Doctor. A group can imply another group with implied_ids, so a manager gets everything a doctor has.
Access rights (ir.model.access): per model and per group, four boxes: read, write, create, delete. A user without any access right on a model gets an access error.
Record rules (ir.rule): a domain that filters the records a group may see or change, for example only the appointments of the current company.

div.p: In om_hospital the access rights are in security/ir.model.access.csv, the first file of the data list in __manifest__.py. Every model, the wizards too, gives all rights to internal users (base.group_user):

pre.code: id,name,model_id:id,group_id:id,perm_read,perm_write,perm_create,perm_unlink access_hospital_patient_user,hospital.patient user,model_hospital_patient,base.group_user,1,1,1,1

div.p: Groups also hide parts of the interface. In views/menus.xml the Settings menu is shown to administrators only:

pre.code: <menuitem id='menu_settings' name='Settings' parent='menu_configuration' action='action_hospital_settings' groups='base.group_system'/>

div.p: A record rule is an XML record. This one, which you can add, limits appointments to the companies selected by the user (hospital.appointment has a company_id field):

pre.code: <record id='hospital_appointment_company_rule' model='ir.rule'> <field name='name'>Appointment: multi-company</field> <field name='model_id' ref='model_hospital_appointment'/> <field name='domain_force'>[('company_id', 'in', company_ids)]</field> </record>

div.p: A rule without groups is global: it applies to everybody and is combined with AND. Rules with groups are combined with OR between the groups of the user. Load the security files before the views in the manifest, so the groups exist when a view or menu refers to them.

Inheritance: change Odoo without touching it

div.p: Inheritance lets you change a model or a view of another module without touching its code. You will use it every day: Odoo itself is built this way.

With _inherit and no _name, you extend the existing model: new fields are added to its table and your methods are added on top of the original ones. In om_hospital, models/sale_order.py adds a field to the sale order:

To change a method, define it again in your class and call super() to run the original code. om_hospital does this in hospital.patient: create() sets the reference from a sequence, then calls super().create(vals_list), and default_get() fills the note after super().default_get(fields_list). Forget super() and the original code does not run at all.

An inherited view has an inherit_id and an arch made of xpath elements. Each one finds a node and puts your content before, after, inside it, or replaces it, or changes its attributes. From views/sale_order_views.xml:

div.p: A module brings its records with it in data files, listed in the data key of __manifest__.py and loaded in that order at install and at every upgrade.

Each <record> has a model and an id, the external id (XML id) that lets Odoo find the record again on the next upgrade. In om_hospital, data/sequence_data.xml creates the patient and appointment sequences and two patient tags:

pre.code: <odoo noupdate='1'> <record id='patient_tag_vip' model='patient.tag'> <field name='name'>VIP</field> <field name='color'>3</field> </record> </odoo>

div.p: A CSV file is named after its model (patient.tag.csv, ir.model.access.csv). The first line holds field names, the id column the XML ids, and a field_id:id column a reference to another XML id. CSV is short for many simple records.

By default an upgrade writes the file values again over the record. With noupdate='1' the records are created once, at install, and then left alone: the next number of a sequence or a tag a user renamed is kept. forcecreate='0' on a record skips it when it does not exist yet in update mode.

div.p: A PDF report in Odoo has two parts: a report action (a record of ir.actions.report) and a QWeb template that builds the HTML. Odoo then turns that HTML into a PDF. The action adds a Print menu entry on the model; the template decides what the page shows.

Open om_hospital/report/patient_card.xml. It holds the action action_report_patient_card on hospital.patient and the template report_patient_card. The template loops on docs (the selected patients), wraps each one in web.external_layout (company header and footer), and prints the fields reference, name, age, gender and responsible_id.

pre.code: <record id='action_report_patient_card' model='ir.actions.report'> <field name='name'>Patient Card</field> <field name='model'>hospital.patient</field> <field name='report_type'>qweb-pdf</field> <field name='report_name'>om_hospital.report_patient_card</field> <field name='print_report_name'>'Patient Card - %s' % object.name</field> <field name='binding_model_id' ref='model_hospital_patient'/> <field name='binding_type'>report</field> </record>

A server action and a Python method that writes a PDF file
You can do this by hand, but the standard way is a report action with a QWeb template.

The hospital.patient records selected for printing
Odoo passes the records the user prints as docs; the template loops on them.

The company that prints the report

div.p: Every om_hospital model inherits mail.thread and mail.activity.mixin. That gives each record a chatter: messages, followers, activities and a log of field changes. This section shows how to fill the chatter from code and how to send emails.

In om_hospital/models/appointment.py, the fields patient_id, doctor_id and state have tracking=True: when they change, Odoo posts the old and the new value in the chatter. tracking also takes a number: lower numbers are shown first.

pre.code: state = fields.Selection([...], string='Status', default='draft', required=True, tracking=1) patient_id = fields.Many2one('hospital.patient', required=True, tracking=2)

div.p: message_post() adds a message to the record. A plain string is escaped; wrap HTML in Markup so the tags are kept. Use subtype_xmlid='mail.mt_note' for an internal note.

pre.code: from markupsafe import Markup def action_confirm(self): self.write({'state': 'confirm'}) for appointment in self: appointment.message_post( body=Markup('Appointment %s is confirmed.') % appointment.name, subtype_xmlid='mail.mt_note')

pre.code:
Appointment: Confirmation Appointment {{ object.name }} {{ object.patient_id.responsible_id.id }}

Your appointment with is confirmed.

div.p: Send it with template.send_mail(appointment.id, force_send=True), or post it in the chatter with appointment.message_post_with_source(template).

record.field: What does tracking=True on a field of a mail.thread model do?
It logs the old and the new value in the chatter when the field changes
Tracking writes a message with the change, so you see who changed what and when.
It sends an email to the followers for every change
Tracking logs the change in the chatter; emails depend on the subtype and followers.
It makes the field read-only after the first save
Tracking has nothing to do with read-only.
It adds the field to the search view
Search views are defined in XML.
Two fields have tracking=1 and tracking=5. Which change is shown first in the message?
Lower numbers come first; True counts as 100.
The field that was changed first
The order comes from the numbers, not from the time of the change.
You call message_post(body='Confirmed') with a plain Python string. What does the chatter show?
The tags as text, because a plain string is escaped; use Markup to keep the HTML
message_post escapes str bodies; a Markup object is kept as HTML.
An error, because body must be a list
body is a string or a Markup object.
Nothing, because the message is empty
The message is posted; only the tags are escaped.
In the body_html of a mail.template, how do you print the name of the record?
body_html is rendered with QWeb and object is the record.
This is the old Jinja-like syntax; it is no longer used.
{{ }} is used in fields like subject, and the variable is object, not record.
Python format strings are not rendered in templates.

div.p: Integrations let Odoo talk to other systems over HTTP. This section covers three tools: webhooks in automation rules, controllers you write in Python, and the read-only URLs Odoo gives you for data and documentation.
Webhooks come with the Automation Rules app (module base_automation; om_hospital does not depend on it, so install it first). There are two directions:

ul.li: Send: an automation rule on hospital.appointment (for example when state becomes Confirmed) with the action Send Webhook Notification. Odoo POSTs the chosen fields as JSON to the URL you give.
Receive: an automation rule with the trigger On webhook. Odoo shows a URL like /web/hook/<uuid>. Another system calls it; the JSON body is available as payload in an Execute Code action.

div.p: Keep the URL secret: anyone who knows it can call the rule. Tick Log Calls while you test.

For full control, write a controller: a Python method with @http.route. type='http' returns a page or a file; type='json' reads a JSON-RPC body and returns JSON. om_hospital has no controller yet; you would add om_hospital/controllers/main.py and import it in __init__.py.

The two short videos show newer helpers: a /json/ URL that returns the records of a screen as JSON, and the /doc page that lists the models, fields and methods of your database. The /json/ URL is experimental: it works only on a database with demo data or with the system parameter web.json.enabled, and the user needs export rights.
Sends record data to another system with the Send Webhook Notification action, and receives data with an automation rule triggered On webhook.
Recorded on Odoo 17.

record.field: You want Odoo to receive data from another system without writing Python in a module. What do you use?
An automation rule with the trigger On webhook
Odoo gives the rule a /web/hook/<uuid> URL; the JSON body is available as payload in its actions.
A scheduled action runs at intervals; it does not receive calls.
Email templates send emails; they do not receive data.
What does the action Send Webhook Notification do?
It POSTs the chosen fields of the record as JSON to a URL
You pick the URL and the fields; Odoo sends them when the rule runs.
It sends an email to the followers
That is the Send Email action.
It creates a new automation rule
It is one action of a rule, not a way to create rules.
It opens a URL in the user's browser
The request is sent by the server, not opened in the browser.
Why should the URL of an On webhook rule be kept secret?
Anyone who knows it can trigger the rule, without logging in
The webhook route is public; the uuid in the URL is the protection. You can rotate it if it leaks.
Because it contains the admin password
The URL contains a random uuid, not a password.
Because it stops working once it is shared
It keeps working until you rotate the uuid.
In a controller, what is the difference between type='http' and a JSON route?
type='http' returns pages or files; a JSON route reads a JSON-RPC request and returns the result as JSON
Use http for pages, downloads and forms; use the JSON type for calls from JavaScript or other programs.
type='http' needs a login and a JSON route does not
Login is set by auth (user, public, none), not by the type.
There is no difference, both return HTML
A JSON route serializes the return value to JSON.
A JSON route works only for the website
Both types work for the backend and the website.
External API: om_hospital from a script

div.p: The external API lets a program outside Odoo (a script, a website, another ERP) log in and work with records: search, read, create, write and delete. Every public method of a model can be called, with the access rights of the user who logs in.

ol.li: Call authenticate on /xmlrpc/2/common with the database, login and password (or API key). You get the user id (uid).
Call execute_kw on /xmlrpc/2/object with the database, uid, password, model, method, a list of positional arguments and a dict of keyword arguments.

pre.code:
import xmlrpc.client
url, db = 'http://localhost:8069', 'my_db' username, password = 'admin', 'my-api-key'
common = xmlrpc.client.ServerProxy(f'{url}/xmlrpc/2/common') uid = common.authenticate(db, username, password, {}) models = xmlrpc.client.ServerProxy(f'{url}/xmlrpc/2/object')
patients = models.execute_kw(db, uid, password, 'hospital.patient', 'search_read', [[('gender', '=', 'female')]], {'fields': ['reference', 'name', 'age'], 'limit': 5})

div.p: The model names and fields are the ones of om_hospital/models: hospital.patient (name, date_of_birth, gender, tag_ids), hospital.doctor (doctor_name, speciality) and hospital.appointment (patient_id, doctor_id, date_appointment, state). Rules of the models still apply from outside: create sets the patient reference from the sequence, and deleting an appointment that is done raises an error.

pre.code: new_id = models.execute_kw(db, uid, password, 'hospital.patient', 'create', [{'name': 'Jane Doe', 'gender': 'female', 'date_of_birth': '1990-05-01'}]) models.execute_kw(db, uid, password, 'hospital.patient', 'write', [[new_id], {'note': 'Created from a script'}]) models.execute_kw(db, uid, password, 'hospital.patient', 'unlink', [[new_id]])

div.p: Do not put a real password in a script. Create an API key in Preferences > Account Security > New API Key and use it in place of the password. It works with the same calls and you can revoke it at any time. The same calls also exist over JSON-RPC at /jsonrpc.

field.name: description
field.div: Look under the hood of Odoo: query its PostgreSQL database, read and fix common errors, and run Odoo on a real server with Nginx, HTTPS, workers and backups, or on Odoo.sh. You also set up the tools that make daily work faster, and learn how to publish a module on the Apps Store.

div.p: Every Odoo database is a PostgreSQL database. The ORM turns each model into a table and each stored field into a column, so you can look at your data directly with psql or pgAdmin. This section shows how to create the database user Odoo connects with, how to browse the tables, how to write basic queries, and how to run SQL from Python when the ORM is not enough.

ul.li: hospital.patient (models/patient.py) is the table hospital_patient, with columns such as reference, name, gender, date_of_birth and age (a computed field, but store=True, so it has a column).
hospital.appointment is hospital_appointment; its Many2one patient_id is an integer column that holds the id of a row of hospital_patient.
The Many2many tag_ids lives in a relation table, hospital_patient_patient_tag_rel, with the columns hospital_patient_id and patient_tag_id.
One2many fields such as appointment_ids and non-stored computed fields such as appointment_count have no column.

pre.code: SELECT reference, name, age FROM hospital_patient WHERE gender = 'female' AND active ORDER BY name;

div.p: om_hospital itself uses the ORM only (see _read_group in _compute_appointment_count). When you do need SQL, use the cursor of the environment, pass values as parameters (never format them into the string), and flush the fields you read first, because the ORM keeps pending writes in memory:

pre.code:
from odoo.tools import SQL
self.env['hospital.patient'].flush_model(['age']) self.env.cr.execute(SQL( "SELECT id, name FROM hospital_patient WHERE age < %s", 18)) kids = self.env.cr.dictfetchall()

div.p: Raw SQL skips access rights, record rules and computed field updates. Keep it for reports and large reads, and write through the ORM.

Odoo 18:
Odoo 18 adds self.env.execute_query(SQL(...)) and self.env.execute_query_dict(SQL(...)): they run the query and return the rows, and flush the fields passed as to_flush to SQL.

record.field: How To Execute SQL Queries In Odoo

div.p: Runs SQL queries from Python code in Odoo with the cursor and reads the results with fetchall and dictfetchall.
div.div:
In Odoo 18, this works a little differently from the video:
Odoo 17:
Odoo 17 adds odoo.tools.SQL, a wrapper that keeps the query and its parameters together and that cr.execute accepts: self.env.cr.execute(SQL("SELECT id, name FROM hospital_patient WHERE gender = %s", 'male')). The model method flush() is gone: call self.env['hospital.patient'].flush_model(), records.flush_recordset() or self.env.flush_all() before reading with SQL.
Odoo 18:
Odoo 18 adds self.env.execute_query(SQL(...)), which returns a list of tuples, and self.env.execute_query_dict(SQL(...)), which returns a list of dicts. They flush the fields given in the to_flush argument of SQL, for example SQL("SELECT %s FROM hospital_patient", SQL.identifier('age'), to_flush=self._fields['age']).

record.field: In which table does PostgreSQL store the records of the model hospital.patient?
Odoo replaces the dots of the model name with underscores to name the table.
Dots are not used in table names: the table is hospital_patient.
ir_model lists the models, it does not hold their records.
Patients are a model of their own in om_hospital, not partners.
Why should Odoo connect with its own database user instead of postgres?
postgres is a superuser; Odoo even refuses to start with it, as a security risk
A dedicated user limits the damage if Odoo is compromised, and Odoo aborts when db_user is postgres.
postgres can do everything; that is the problem.
Because Odoo needs a user named odoo
Any name works: you set it with db_user.
Because pgAdmin cannot connect as postgres
pgAdmin can; this is about the Odoo server.
You change a patient with write() and then read the same column with cr.execute in the same method. What must you do first?
Flush the field, so the pending write reaches the database
The ORM keeps writes in memory until a flush; flush_model() or flush_recordset() sends them before your query.
Committing in model code breaks the transaction handling of Odoo; a flush is enough.
Nothing, the write is already in the table
Not always: writes are delayed until the ORM flushes.
The server has nothing to do with it.
Which way of passing a value to a query is safe?
self.env.cr.execute("SELECT id FROM hospital_patient WHERE name = %s", (name,))
The driver escapes parameters, so the value cannot change the query. SQL("... %s", name) does the same.
self.env.cr.execute(f"SELECT id FROM hospital_patient WHERE name = '{name}'")
Formatting the value into the string allows SQL injection.
self.env.cr.execute("SELECT id FROM hospital_patient WHERE name = '%s'" % name)
The % operator formats the string before the driver sees it: same injection risk.

div.p: Errors are part of development. This section teaches you to read them instead of guessing: where Odoo prints the traceback, how to find the line of your own module in it, and how to fix three errors you will meet early. The last lesson shows upgrade_code, the command that rewrites your code for a newer Odoo.

ul.li: Run the server in a terminal (or set logfile and read the log). The last line of a traceback is the error; the lines above show where it happened. Look for the first line in your own module, for example om_hospital/models/patient.py.
Errors in XML files appear when you install or upgrade the module (-u om_hospital), with the file name and the faulty element.
Use _logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) and _logger.info(...) rather than print, and breakpoint() to stop in the debugger.

div.p: A compute method must give a value to every record in self, in every branch. _compute_age in models/patient.py assigns 0 when there is no date of birth:

On a server everything is set in a config file, read with -c. A typical file for one instance:

pre.code: [options] admin_passwd = a-long-random-password db_host = localhost db_port = 5432 db_user = odoo17 db_password = secret addons_path = /opt/odoo17/odoo/addons,/opt/odoo17/custom-addons http_port = 8069 gevent_port = 8072 proxy_mode = True workers = 5 max_cron_threads = 1 dbfilter = ^%d$ logfile = /var/log/odoo/odoo17.log

ul.li: workers: 0 runs Odoo in threads (for development). Above 0, Odoo starts that many HTTP processes plus a gevent process on gevent_port for the live notifications (websocket). A common start is CPU cores x 2 + 1, limited by RAM and the limit_memory_* options.
proxy_mode: set it when Nginx is in front, so Odoo trusts the X-Forwarded headers (client IP, https).
dbfilter: chooses the database from the host name; %d is the first part of the domain, %h the whole host.

field.div: A migration guide for module developers, one section per version of Odoo: the code changes you must make when you move a module from the version before, with the old and the new code side by side, plus short videos on what is new in the interface.

record.field: From Odoo 16 to Odoo 17: the developer checklist

div.p: Moving a module from Odoo 16 to Odoo 17? Go through this checklist, most important first. om_hospital 17.0 already uses the new way everywhere, so its files are good examples.
div.h4: 1. Views: attrs and states are gone
div.p: Odoo 17 refuses a view that still has attrs or states: "Since 17.0, the attrs and states attributes are no longer used". Write the condition as a Python expression directly in invisible, readonly or required. See views/appointment_views.xml.

pre.code: <button name="action_confirm" type="object" states="draft"/> <field name="patient_id" attrs="{'readonly': [('state', '!=', 'draft')]}"/>
<button name="action_confirm" type="object" invisible="state != 'draft'"/> <field name="patient_id" readonly="state != 'draft'"/>

div.h4: 2. Views: column_invisible is its own attribute
div.p: To hide a column of a list, use column_invisible with an expression, not a key inside attrs.

pre.code: <field name="qty" attrs="{'column_invisible': [('parent.state', '=', 'done')]}"/>
<field name="qty" column_invisible="parent.state == 'done'"/>

div.h4: 3. Fields: no more states= in Python
div.p: The states parameter of a field is no longer supported (Odoo logs a warning and ignores it). Move the condition to the view.

pre.code: name = fields.Char(readonly=True, states={'draft': [('readonly', False)]})
name = fields.Char() # in the form view: <field name="name" readonly="state != 'draft'"/>

div.p: name_get() is deprecated. Override _compute_display_name() and set display_name, as models/patient.py does.

pre.code: def name_get(self): return [(p.id, '[%s] %s' % (p.reference, p.name)) for p in self]

div.p: _name_search() lost name_get_uid, takes domain and order, and returns ids or a query. Often you do not need it at all: set _rec_names_search, like hospital.patient.

pre.code: def _name_search(self, name='', args=None, operator='ilike', limit=100, name_get_uid=None):
def _name_search(self, name, domain=None, operator='ilike', limit=None, order=None):

div.p: _read_group() now takes groupby and aggregates lists and returns tuples with records, not dictionaries. See _compute_appointment_count in models/patient.py.
A post_init_hook (and the uninstall hook) gets one argument, env, instead of cr, registry.

pre.code: def post_init_hook(cr, registry): env = api.Environment(cr, SUPERUSER_ID, {})
def post_init_hook(env): ...

div.h4: 8. JavaScript: a field widget is registered as an object
div.p: The fields registry now holds an object with a component key (plus options such as supportedTypes), not the component class itself.

pre.code: registry.category("fields").add("my_char", MyCharField);
export const myCharField = { component: MyCharField, supportedTypes: ["char"] }; registry.category("fields").add("my_char", myCharField);

div.h4: 9. JavaScript: no legacy odoo.define() left in the web client
div.p: In Odoo 16, web/static/src still had over a hundred legacy odoo.define() modules; in Odoo 17 it has none. Write your code as ES modules with Owl components.

pre.code: /** @odoo-module **/ import { Component } from "@odoo/owl";

div.p: The odoo-bin commands are the same as in Odoo 16, so your scripts keep working.

pre.code: def _name_search(self, name, domain=None, operator='ilike', limit=None, order=None):
def _search_display_name(self, operator, value): return ['|', ('name', operator, value), ('reference', operator, value)]
